region: Capital city in Republic of the Congo
heroText: Brazzaville is the Republic of the Congo's capital, spread along the north bank of the Congo River directly across from Kinshasa. First-time visitors should see the Basilique Sainte-Anne du Congo for its striking green-tiled roof, browse artists' studios in Poto-Poto, and pay respects at the Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza Memorial on the riverside Corniche. Maya-Maya Airport keeps the city connected to Paris and the region, and a river ferry links Brazzaville directly to Kinshasa.

areas.name: Poto-Poto
areas.text: Poto-Poto is Brazzaville's historic arts quarter, home to the famous Poto-Poto School of Painting and lively markets, ideal for culture-focused stays.

areas.name: Bacongo
areas.text: Bacongo is a traditional neighborhood known as the home of La Sape, Congo's flamboyant dandy fashion movement, with tailors and lively street life.

areas.name: Centre-Ville / Plateau
areas.text: The Centre-Ville and Plateau area holds government buildings, banks and the main hotels, the most convenient base for business travel.

areas.name: Moungali
areas.text: Moungali is a busy residential and commercial district north of the centre, useful for longer stays close to local markets and transport links.

airports.name: Maya-Maya Airport (BZV)
airports.search: Maya-Maya Airport, Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo
airports.text: Maya-Maya Airport sits just west of downtown Brazzaville, with flights to Paris, Kinshasa and regional cities and taxis available outside arrivals.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Maya-Maya Airport (BZV) and central Brazzaville before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Stay in Centre-Ville or Plateau for an easy first visit close to hotels, banks and government offices, then explore Poto-Poto for art studios and markets or Bacongo for La Sape culture and nightlife. Moungali suits longer stays wanting a quieter, more local base.
hotelIntro: Brazzaville hotel choice depends on purpose: Centre-Ville and Plateau suit business travelers needing central hotels near government offices, Poto-Poto and Bacongo suit visitors wanting art, markets and nightlife, and Moungali suits longer, quieter stays near local transport.
rentalCars: A rental car with driver helps for trips beyond the centre, such as reaching the river ferry terminal or nearby nature reserves, though taxis cover downtown Brazzaville well.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Centre-Ville or Plateau for an easy first stay close to hotels, banks and the riverside Corniche without needing a car.

travelTips.title: Kinshasa ferry
travelTips.text: Consider a day trip across the Congo River to Kinshasa by ferry, but carry passports and visas since it counts as international travel.

travelTips.title: Airport transfers
travelTips.text: Arrange a hotel pickup at Maya-Maya Airport in advance, since taxis outside arrivals can be limited late at night.

travelTips.title: Cash and language
travelTips.text: Carry Central African CFA francs for everyday purchases and expect French as the main working language across hotels and markets.

history.label: Origins
history.text: In precolonial times, the location of the modern-day city of Brazzaville was inhabited by two trading centres, Mfwa and Mpila, which were part of the Tio Kingdom (the Eastern Teke).
The Italian-born explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, who was granted French citizenship in 1874, officially founded the settlement on 10 September 1880; it commemorates his name.
From October 1880 until May 1882, a small squad of troops led by Senegalese Sergeant Malamine Camara occupied the site, in order to prevent the land from falling into Belgian hands.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 placed French control over this area on an official footing.
The city became the capital of the French Congo in 1904.
It continued as capital when French Equatorial Africa was founded in 1910, as a federation of French colonial states: it included Gabon, the Central African Republic, and Chad until 1960.
Construction of the railway resulted in the deaths of more than 17,000 Africans, and the people revolted against the French in 1928.
In 1934, the Congo–Ocean Railway opened, linking Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire and bypassing the rapids on the Congo River.
The city served as the capital of Free France from 1940 to 1943.
In 1944, Brazzaville hosted a meeting of the French resistance forces and representatives of France's African colonies.
In 1980, it became a "commune" separated from the surrounding Pool Department and divided into nine "arrondissements" along the French model of administration.

history.label: Growth
history.text: Brazzaville was founded by the French colonial empire upon an existing indigenous Bateke settlement called Ncuna, during the Scramble for Africa when European nations established spheres of influence on the continent.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: During World War II, Brazzaville and the rest of French Equatorial Africa remained beyond the control of Vichy France, which served the Nazi occupation.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: More recently thousands of people leaving the DRC have made their way to Brazzaville; the local United Nations force and the DRC government have accused the city of deporting thousands of these refugees.
